newsitem.title: THAILAND: Small borrowers seen hit by new Thai bank measure.
newsitem.headline: Small borrowers seen hit by new Thai bank measure.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand's latest move to limit foreign loans granted through offshore banking units of Thai banks will have an impact on most banks' lending activities and hit small borrowers, analysts said.

"The new measure will enable only large corporations to mobilise offshore funds. It's very hard for small-sized companies to borrow offshore loans under the new rules," said a senior banker at a local bank.

The Bank of Thailand on Friday issued a circular to Thai commercial banks's units operating under the Bangkok International Banking Facility (BIBF) to curb their loans brought in for relending to Thai-based clients.

The central bank circular said the rise of out-in loans extended by offshore banking units during September-December this year is limited to seven percent of the increase of baht-denominated loans they lend out over the same period.
Out-in loans refer to foreign funds that offshore banks import for relending to local clients.
The central bank also raised, to $US5 million from $2 million, the minimum out-in loan that licensed offshore banking units can extend to new local clients, effective December 1, 1996.

The central bank's new measures would also raise the cost of borrowing offshore funds and put upward pressure on the local interest rates as domestic borrowers will turn to borrow in local currencies, they added.
"The measure will also put some pressure to the local interest rates by sustaining the non-declining trend," the economist Charl Kengchon at Thai Farmers Research Center told Reuters.
Charl said the expected strong demand for baht loans will prompt commercial banks to offer higher deposit rates in an attempt to boost deposits to keep up with the rising credit extension.
